The two revealed dice sum to 5, so the expected value of the remaining six dice is \(6\times3.5=21\).  
Hence the public expectation \(M = 5+21 = 26\).

The informed trader (30 % chance) knows the true total \(V\sim N(26,\,\sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma\approx4.18\).  
The noise trader (70 % chance) has a private valuation \(u\sim N(26,4^2)\) and trades a random quantity \(D\sim\text{Unif}\{1,\dots,5\}\).

For a symmetric quote \( \text{bid}=26-x,\; \text{ask}=26+x\) with unit size on each side, the expected profit per round is  

\[
\Pi(x)=2\Big[0.7\,x\bigl(1-\Phi(x/4)\bigr)-0.3\,\sigma\,\phi(x/\sigma)\Big],
\]

where \(\Phi,\phi\) are the standard normal cdf and pdf.  
Maximising \(\Pi(x)\) gives an optimum near \(x\approx4\).  
With \(x=4\) the expected profit is about +0.25 per round, while any larger size makes the informed‑trader loss dominate.

Thus a good risk‑neutral quote for round 3 is a tight‑size, wide‑spread quote centred at 26.

```json
{"bid": 22.0, "bid_size": 1, "ask": 30.0, "ask_size": 1}
```

The public dice sum to \(3+4+6 = 13\). With five dice still hidden, the expected value of the total \(V\) is  

\[
M = 13 + 5 \times 3.5 = 30.5 .
\]

The distribution of the remaining sum is symmetric around \(M\) with standard deviation \(\sigma_V \approx 3.82\).  
An informed trader (30 % chance) will exploit any quote that crosses the true \(V\); a noise trader (70 % chance) trades when his private valuation \(u = M+e\) (\(e\sim N(0,4^2)\)) lies beyond our quote.

Maximising the expected profit per unit of size gives an optimal half‑spread \(\delta\) of about 6 – 7.  Using a symmetric quote around \(M\) with \(\delta = 6\) yields a positive expected edge while keeping the spread wide enough to deter the informed trader.

Hence I will post a symmetric two‑sided quote centred at \(M=30.5\) with a half‑spread of 6.0 and the maximum size (10) on each side.

```json
{"bid": 24.5, "bid_size": 10, "ask": 36.5, "ask_size": 10}
```

The four revealed dice sum to \(6+5+6+6 = 23\).  
Four dice remain hidden, each with mean 3.5, so the public‑information expectation of the final total is  

\[
M = 23 + 4\times3.5 = 37 .
\]

The hidden‑dice sum has variance \(4\times\frac{35}{12}\approx11.67\) (sd ≈ 3.4).  
With a 30 % chance of an informed trader each round, we want a modest spread around \(M\) to limit adverse selection, while also using our short position (‑6) to bias the quote toward buying back.

A symmetric spread of about 2 points (≈ 0.6 σ) gives a reasonable trade‑off.  
We set the bid a little below \(M\) and the ask a little above \(M\), with enough size to cover the existing short.

\[
\text{bid}=36.0,\quad \text{bid\_size}=6,\qquad
\text{ask}=38.0,\quad \text{ask\_size}=6
\]

```json
{"bid": 36.0, "bid_size": 6, "ask": 38.0, "ask_size": 6}
```

The five revealed dice sum to \(4+6+6+2+2 = 20\).  
The three hidden dice have mean \(3\times3.5 = 10.5\), so the public expectation of the final value is  

\[
M = 20 + 10.5 = 30.5 .
\]

The distribution of the remaining sum (three dice) has variance \(3\times\frac{35}{12}\approx 8.75\) (sd \(\sigma\approx2.96\)).  

With a 30 % chance of an informed trader (who knows \(V\) exactly) and a 70 % chance of a noise trader (valuation \(u=M+e,\;e\sim N(0,4^2)\)), the expected marginal profit from a unit posted on the ask at price \(A\) and on the bid at price \(B\) can be written (using the normal approximation for \(V\)) as  

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pi_{\text{informed}} &= 0.3\;10\Big[ P(V>A)(A-E[V|V>A]) + P(V<B)(E[V|V<B]-B) \Big],\\
\Pi_{\text{noise}}   &= 0.7\;3\Big[ P(u>A)(A-M) + P(u<B)(M-B) \Big],
\end{aligned}
\]

where the noise trade size has expectation \(E[\min(D,10)]=3\) ( \(D\sim\text{Unif}\{1,\dots,5\}\) ).

Evaluating this expression for symmetric quotes \(B=M-d,\;A=M+d\) shows the expected profit is maximised near \(d\approx4.5\).  
Choosing one‑decimal prices gives \(B=26.0,\;A=35.0\).  
Both sides are given the maximum size (10) because only one counterparty arrives per round, so the size only caps the possible trade.

\[
\boxed{\{"bid":26.0,"bid\_size":10,"ask":35.0,"ask\_size":10\}}
\]

The public dice sum to 11, leaving four hidden dice (mean 14, sd≈3.42).  
The expected value of V is therefore 25.  

With a long position of +5 bought at 24, the current expected profit from inventory is 5 × (25‑24)= 5.  
To increase expected profit we should sell to noise traders (who buy when their private valuation u > 25) while limiting adverse‑selection losses to informed traders (who buy only when V > ask).  

Optimising the ask price a with a full ask size of 5 (the maximum noise demand) gives the highest expected marginal profit around a ≈ 30. At a = 30 the expected gain from noise buyers (~1.11) exceeds the expected loss to informed traders (~0.70).  

Since we are already long, we do not want to post a bid. Setting bid size 0 removes any bid‑side exposure.

**Quote for round 5**

```json
{"bid": 0, "bid_size": 0, "ask": 30.0, "ask_size": 5}
```
